turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Maeve, before you go in, blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, pulse eighty-eight, temperature thirty-six point eight, and oxygen ninety-eight percent. You're looking tired, love.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I am tired. I've been clawing at myself half the night and that waiting room is like a sauna. Are we going in or what?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor's free now. Is your sister coming in with you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): She wouldn't stay in the car. Come on so, Niamh.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello Maeve, hello Niamh. Sit wherever you like. What's brought you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): This rash. It's itching the life out of me, I haven't slept, and I'm in foul form, so you'll have to bear with me.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll take it handy. When did you first notice the rash?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The drive was a nightmare, some eejit on the M50, and then reception had me standing there while they hunted the chart, so I'm already—
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Maeve. He asked when it started, not about the M50.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I heard him the first time. I can't put a date on it. It was after the long weekend, or maybe before it, I honestly don't know. Don't write a day down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand, we'll leave the date open. Whereabouts is it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Both arms, and across the belly. Red, with wee bumps, and the itch is savage. The arms are worse than the stomach.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was scratching at her chest yesterday as well—
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the label in the jumper, Niamh, not a rash. The chest is fine.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Alright, maybe the jumper. I'll hush.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the lips or the tongue? Any tightness when you breathe?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, and no trouble breathing. I'd have told you.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish, hot or shivery?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm just wrecked.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the itch worse at any particular time of day?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): The neighbour's dog was barking till all hours, which did nothing for my mood. Useless yoke of an animal.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You can't blame the dog for a rash.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not blaming the dog. It's worse at night, when I'm trying to sleep. That's what you asked.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right so. Anything new lately, food or a cream or a tablet?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the bit that's doing my head in. I had prawns, there's a new cream, and I'm on an antibiotic, and I haven't a clue which of them did this.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't jump at one. Which antibiotic are you on?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The one for the sinus. Amox— I always mangle it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Amoxicillin. Five hundred milligrams, three times a day, from the chemist on the main street.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I was getting there. Amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, by mouth, for the sinus. I am taking it.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you start the tablets?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't give you a date for those either. A few days, could be a week, I never wrote it down. The sinus itself was last winter, or the one before — I'm mixing the two of them up.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you getting all three doses in?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I missed yesterday morning, I was dead asleep. The rest I've taken. So not perfectly, no.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the cream before it goes out of your head.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not going out of my head. New cream, white tub, from Boots. I think it says Cetraben, but I hadn't my glasses and I wouldn't swear to the name.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): What did you pick it up for?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry skin on the arms. I started it round the same time as this rash, which is no help to anyone.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the prawns. What happened after them?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a takeaway. I felt a bit queasy after, nothing dramatic, and I've eaten prawns my whole life. I don't think it was them, but I can't rule it out, and I won't put a date on the takeaway either.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines? Sprays, painkillers, anything else from the GP?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol for the sinus headache, two five-hundred tablets when I need them, not every day. And I stopped the brown nose spray, Flixonase. That was weeks ago. It was doing nothing.
[SEG0042] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You were on that spray for ages.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And I'm not on it now. Weeks ago. Leave it, Niamh.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Niamh, you look like you're holding something back.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the penicillin. When she was small they gave her penicillin and she came out in a rash, head to toe. Mam kept her off it after that.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): That did not happen to me. I have no penicillin allergy. Mam mixed me up with our cousin Orla. I've taken penicillin plenty of times since.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): So you're telling me there's no penicillin allergy, and Niamh remembers a rash from it when you were a child.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm telling you it wasn't me. I'm tired, not confused.
[SEG0049] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I was in the room, Maeve. You were covered. I'm not backing down.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. I won't record it as a definite allergy, and I won't pretend I didn't hear it either. Did anyone ever actually test you, bloods or skin tests?

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Years ago in the hospital, and don't ask me the year because I haven't a clue, they did an allergy blood test and they said it was borderline. No number. They just said borderline, and then nothing came of it.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline, as you remember it, with no figure. I'll note that, but I can't treat it as a result I can stand over.

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. The forearms and the lower abdomen are red, with scattered raised bumps, no blisters, and the skin isn't broken. Lips and tongue look normal. Your chest is clear when I listen, no wheeze.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): The belly is itchier than it looks. Don't be poking at it.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to hang this on one cause today. It might be a drug rash from the amoxicillin, or a reaction to that cream, or the prawns, and I can't separate the three of them on what I can see.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): So you've no idea. Brilliant. I took the morning off work for that.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): I know that's maddening. What we can do is settle the itch and not feed it. I'd like you to stop the amoxicillin from today, and don't take another dose.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): And what about the sinus, then?
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): The sinus can sit for a few days. We'll not start another antibiotic today. For the itch I'll prescribe cetirizine, ten milligrams, once a day, by mouth.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): We might arrange patch testing if the rash hasn't settled when I see you next. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in a fortnight. If your lips swell or your breathing goes tight, go to A&E rather than waiting on me.
